memo.thesis_en: I own these shares, bought a week ago at $251.845 and now marked down about 11%. A price decline with no change in the business is not a sell trigger. It is the market offering me the same company for less. The numbers I can see are good: five-year average ROE of 26.9%, debt-to-equity of 0.32, and owner earnings averaging about $9.26 billion against a $134 billion market cap. But I would not lean on the 49.86% margin of safety. It rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate, which is a generous setup, and the snapshot says nothing about ten years of earnings, CEO tenure or moat metrics. So I keep what I have, add nothing until I can confirm those gaps, and watch whether technology change erodes the consulting franchise.

Clients hire it to redesign processes, build and run software systems, and manage large transformation programs. The business needs little capital, so owner earnings run high relative to book value, and the snapshot shows about $9.26 billion averaged over five years. The risks are cyclical corporate spending on discretionary projects and technology shifts, such as automation, that could shrink demand for labor-based services. Those make it a business I can understand but cannot forecast with the certainty I want.

memo.thesis_en: The screen numbers look good: a 45% margin of safety, a 22% five-year average ROE and debt-to-equity of 0.43. But I don't own this name, and a cheap price alone doesn't get me to buy. The snapshot gives me only a ticker, with no business description, no moat evidence and no earnings history. I can't write the two-paragraph explanation with the confidence I demand, and I can't confirm a moat that will last ten years. Services businesses that sell labor and process work are exposed to technological change that could make their moat something that has to be rebuilt every year, and I have always said a moat that must be continuously rebuilt is no moat at all. A low price on a business I can't predict is exactly the trap I try to avoid. I'll pass and wait for a pitch squarely in my sweet spot.

memo.thesis_en: I understand this business: it sells other people's consumer electronics and appliances out of big boxes and online. The price looks fair, at $97.14 against a computed value of $117.52, and the numbers clear the screen on size, leverage and a 17% discount. But I can't find a moat. The products are made by someone else, shoppers can compare prices with a phone, and the brand gives no pricing power I can see. A business like that has to earn its return again every year, and the high ROE of 48% looks to me more like a small equity base than a franchise. A cheap price on a retailer with no durable advantage is the cigar-butt thinking I left behind after See's. I'll pass and wait for a better pitch.

memo.two_paragraph_business_description:
As I understand it, NEU is a specialty chemicals company that develops and sells performance additives, the chemical packages blended into fuels and lubricants to improve how they protect, clean and perform inside engines and drivetrains. Customers are oil companies and lubricant marketers, who buy these formulations because they have to work reliably in demanding equipment.

The company makes money by selling these formulated products, usually repeatedly, at prices reflecting the performance and testing behind them rather than raw commodity cost. The economic appeal is high returns on equity with modest capital needs. The risk is that demand depends on the long-term mix of engines and machinery in use, which I can't judge from the numbers I was given.

memo.thesis_en: We own ten shares, bought at $128.38 and now marked at $103.61, down 19.3% after 108 days, and the question is whether to keep them. The numbers in front of me are the kind I like: a 34.6% average ROE over five years, a debt-to-equity of 0.0, and owner earnings of about $1.32 billion against a market cap of about $10.9 billion. The model says $363 a share, but that rests on an 8% growth rate and a 5% discount rate, and I would not bet the farm on a 71% margin of safety from a spreadsheet, so I haircut it heavily. My real worry is that this is a brand tied to apparel fashion, and fashion is a moat that must be rebuilt each season, which is no moat at all if it fails. A lower price does not make me sell, and nothing in this snapshot shows the moat has eroded, so I keep what we own, I do not add until I can confirm ten years of earnings and pricing power, and I stay ready to sell if the brand's economics crack.

The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 17.2% and debt-to-equity of 0.30, both inside my thresholds, and the owner-earnings DCF gives about $417 a share against a $344.62 price, a 17.4% margin of safety. We are down 2.43% after 26 days, which tells me nothing; a price decline with the franchise intact is no reason to sell. I would hold the one share and not add until I could check the data I am missing.

memo.thesis_en: I don't own Adobe, and the numbers in front of me are the kind that make an old man sit up: a 5-year average ROE of 40.0%, debt-to-equity of 0.41, and a price of $221.40 against a computed value of $467.50. But I'd be careful with that margin of safety. It rests on a 5% discount rate and 8% growth, and a small change in those inputs moves it a lot. The bigger question is whether a business built on creative software will still have its pricing power ten years out, now that machines can make images and documents on their own. I can't answer that with the confidence I'd want, and the snapshot doesn't give me the ten-year earnings record or the management history to lean on. So I keep it on the list and wait. If I can't tell where the moat stands in ten years, I'd rather pass than guess.

memo.moat_analysis: The moat I'd attribute to Adobe is switching costs: professionals and enterprises build workflows, file formats and training around its tools, and leaving is costly. The 40.0% 5-year average ROE is consistent with that kind of franchise economics. What I cannot verify from this snapshot is customer retention, pricing-power history, or how well the franchise holds up as AI lowers the cost of creating content. A moat that has to be rebuilt every few years is not a moat, and I can't yet tell which side of that line this falls on.
memo.two_paragraph_business_description:
Adobe sells software that creative professionals, marketers and businesses use to make, edit and manage images, video, documents and digital content. Customers mostly pay recurring subscriptions, so revenue arrives steadily rather than in one-time purchases. The tools are embedded in daily work, and file formats and trained users make switching painful.

The business makes money by charging a subscription fee for access to the software and related cloud services, with very little physical capital required. The profit per dollar of revenue can be high because software is cheap to copy once built. The risk is that new technology, especially AI-generated content, could change who needs these tools and how much they will pay.
